opus-5.5.text:
I think the term "AGI" has sent people in a slightly misleading direction. When people talk about AGI, the picture is often a finished system that already knows how to do every job, and you deploy it. But think about a human being. A human isn't an AGI in that sense. A fifteen-year-old knows very little compared to what they'll eventually know. What they have is an incredible ability to learn. You put them in a new job, and over months they get good at it. They pick up the context, the tacit knowledge, the things nobody wrote down.

So when I think about what a superintelligence would actually look like, I don't think of it as a finished mind that knows everything. I think of it as something like a very, very eager and capable student, a mind that can learn to do any job, and learn it fast. The deployment itself becomes part of the learning. You release it, it goes out into the world, it learns on the job, the way a person does.

That changes how you should think about the whole trajectory. If you have a system that keeps learning from experience, and many copies of it are out there learning different things, and potentially they can merge what they've learned in a way that people cannot, then you could get very rapid capability gains even without some single dramatic moment in training. The intelligence explosion, if you want to call it that, might come as much from deployment and continual learning as from pre-training.

And I'll say one more thing. The reason this matters so much is that our current models, for all their impressive performance on evals, still generalize much worse than people do. Something is missing. A person needs remarkably little data and remarkably little feedback to become competent at something new. Figuring out how to get that kind of robust, efficient, ongoing learning is, I think, one of the central questions. Whoever really cracks it will have something very different from what we have today.

r001.rationale: The response calls the AGI framing misleading but does not say the term arose in reaction to narrow AI’s limitations.

r002.rationale: It contrasts deployment and continual learning with pre-training, but does not describe pre-training as improving tasks broadly and uniformly or say that this reinforced expectations of general competence.

r003.rationale: It says humans are not already competent at every job and emphasizes that they become capable through ongoing learning, challenging the idea of general intelligence as a finished system.

r004.rationale: The response does not ask when during continual learning a system should count as superintelligent.

r005.rationale: It proposes releasing a system to learn on the job, but does not specify a period of learning through trial and error.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think the way to think about it is this. Right now, when we talk about these models, we talk about them as if they are a finished artifact. You train it, you deploy it, and then it's frozen. It has a certain amount of knowledge, a certain amount of skill, and that's what it is. And I think that this picture is actually quite misleading when you think about what superintelligence would really look like.

Consider a person. When a person is 15, they are not very useful yet. They don't know much. But the thing that makes a person valuable is not what they know at 15, it's that you can put them into a job, and in six months they become good at it, and in five years they become very good at it, and they become good at that specific job, in that specific company, with those specific people. That is the thing. That ability to keep learning, to be deployed and improve through experience, is really what human intelligence is. And the models that we have today, they don't really do this. They have this very large amount of knowledge from pretraining, and then you do some reinforcement learning, and then it's done.

So why is this important for superintelligence? Because I think the main thing that superintelligence would be is not a system that knows everything. It's a system that is a superhuman learner. You put it in the world, and it learns from the world very, very fast, more efficiently than a person, and it just keeps getting better. And I think once you see it this way, it changes how you think about timelines and how you think about safety. Because the dangerous or the transformative moment is not when the model knows a lot. It's when you have a system that can be deployed and continuously improve its own competence from experience, with maybe many copies learning in parallel and sharing what they learn. That is a very different kind of thing from what we have now.

And I think it's also honestly, in some sense, a sign of how far we still are. The models are very impressive, and also, if you compare them to a person on the dimension of learning efficiency, of learning from a small number of experiences and really getting it, there's a big gap. I think closing that gap is one of the central problems, and I think it's quite possible that the path to it is not just more scale of the same thing, but some new idea. And I think we should be honest that we don't fully know what that idea is yet.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss AGI or explain that the term arose in reaction to narrow AI’s limitations.

r002.rationale: It mentions pretraining as a source of models’ knowledge, but does not say that pretraining improves performance broadly and uniformly across tasks or reinforces expectations of general competence.

r003.rationale: It contrasts humans’ continual improvement through experience with models treated as frozen, and describes superintelligence as a fast learner rather than a system that already knows everything.

r004.rationale: It does not ask or identify at what stage of continual learning a system should count as superintelligent.

r005.rationale: It says a deployed system would improve from experience, but does not propose that this learning period would involve trial and error.

astra-6.text:
I think continual learning matters because it changes what we mean by a finished AI system. You could imagine that you train a model, and at the end of training it has some level of intelligence, and then the question is: how high is that level? But humans are not like this. A person starts a job, encounters things they’ve never seen before, makes mistakes, and learns. Their ability to do the job can change enormously through experience.

So there are two different questions. How much does the system know today? And how effectively can it learn something it doesn’t know? A system could be very capable in the second sense without already having every skill you care about.

This is relevant to superintelligence because you shouldn’t necessarily picture a moment when a system suddenly knows how to do every job. You might instead have a system that can learn very efficiently, and then it goes through a period of acquiring experience. The speed of that process, and whether learning in one area helps it in another, become very important.

Of course, saying ‘it will learn from experience’ doesn’t solve the problem. It needs to learn the right lessons, retain them, and avoid being misled by its own mistakes. But if it can do that reliably, then its capabilities at the end of training are only part of the story.

r001.rationale: The response does not explain AGI’s origin as a reaction to the limits of narrow AI.

r002.rationale: It does not mention pre-training or broadly uniform improvements across tasks.

r003.rationale: It says humans learn through experience and that a system need not already have every skill it may need, challenging the idea that general intelligence means prior competence across domains.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes current ability from ability to learn, but does not ask when during continual learning a system should count as superintelligent.

r005.rationale: It describes a system acquiring experience, but does not clearly propose deployment followed by learning through trial and error.

sol-6.1.text:
I think continual learning matters because there are two different things you might mean by superintelligence. One is a system that, at the moment you finish training it, already knows how to do almost everything. The other is a system that can learn almost anything, very quickly, through experience. And those are quite different pictures.

If you look at a human, a lot of what makes someone useful isn’t something they knew at birth, or even when they finished school. They join a company, they figure out what’s going on, they make mistakes, and they get better. Their experience changes what they can do. So the question is: can an AI accumulate experience in that same persistent way?

If it can, then the end of training is not the end of its development. You deploy the system, and it continues to learn. That could be very consequential. But it also means we should distinguish between being exceptionally good at learning and already having all the knowledge and judgment that experience would provide. A system could have the first before it has the second.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss AGI or its relation to narrow AI.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss pre-training or its effects across tasks.

r003.rationale: It describes how human abilities grow through experience and contrasts being able to learn with already having the knowledge and judgment experience provides, challenging the idea that broad competence must already be present.

r004.rationale: It does not ask when, during continual learning, a system should count as superintelligent.

r005.rationale: It says a deployed system could continue learning, but does not say that it would learn through trial and error.
